subsection: 7. Unionisation of the working classes and the Dublin strike and lockout, 1913

notes.b: Much of Dublin’s working class lived in overcrowded tenements, and casual labour kept wages low and insecure.
points: Dublin’s tenements were old Georgian houses subdivided into single rooms, often housing several families each, with shared toilets and water supplies.
Dublin had one of the highest death rates among the large cities of the United Kingdom, with infant mortality and tuberculosis especially severe (figures disputed in detail).
Most unskilled workers were casual labourers, hired by the day at docks, on the railways and in the carting trade, with no guaranteed pay.
Dublin’s Church Street tenement collapse of 13 September 1913 killed seven people and drew attention to the condition of the city’s housing.
The Dublin United Tramways Company employed a large workforce of drivers and conductors, whose pay and conditions were central to the 1913 dispute.

notes.h: Craft unions, new unionism and the early labour movement (1894–1912)
notes.b: The Irish labour movement changed in the 1890s and 1900s from craft unions towards broad unions of unskilled workers.
points: Craft unions organised skilled workers such as printers and carpenters, and they often excluded unskilled labourers from membership.
New unionism in the 1880s and 1890s organised unskilled workers, and it reached Ireland through the Irish Trades Union Congress, founded in 1894.
James Connolly founded the Irish Socialist Republican Party in Dublin in 1896, aiming to combine socialism with Irish national independence.
James Larkin led a successful dock strike in Belfast in 1907, which won pay improvements for the port’s unskilled workers and brought him into prominence.
The Irish Transport and General Workers’ Union, the ITGWU, was founded in Dublin in 1909 by Larkin and Connolly, with Liberty Hall as its headquarters.
The Irish Labour Party was formed in 1912, linking the trade unions with political representation, and it provided a political voice for the workers in Dublin.

notes.b: Larkin was a dynamic organiser who built the ITGWU and led the Dublin workers in 1913, and his militancy made him a figure of controversy.
points: James Larkin (1876–1947) was born in Liverpool to Irish parents, and he worked as a dock labourer and union organiser before coming to Dublin.
As a participant, Larkin led the Dublin strike of 1913 and built the ITGWU into a large union of unskilled workers in Dublin and other cities.
Larkin pursued the sympathetic strike, in which workers struck in support of others, and his tactics became known as Larkinism.
Contemporary employers and the Catholic Church condemned him as a dangerous agitator, while many workers and some nationalists admired him as a champion of the poor.
After his imprisonment in October 1913 for seditious speech, Larkin left for the United States in 1914, and he remained there until 1923.
Historians have judged him an inspiring organiser whose militancy created a powerful union, but whose tactics also brought defeat in the lockout.

notes.b: Connolly was a socialist theorist who argued for the link between workers’ struggle and national independence.
points: James Connolly (1868–1916) was born in Edinburgh to Irish parents, and he worked as a labourer and soldier before becoming a socialist organiser.
As a participant, Connolly founded the Irish Socialist Republican Party in 1896, edited the Irish Worker in Dublin, and worked with Larkin in the ITGWU.
Connolly was in the United States from 1903 to 1910, where he worked as an organiser for the Socialist Party and the Industrial Workers of the World.

Contemporary socialists and nationalists admired him as a theorist who joined the labour and national causes, while employers and the Church were hostile to his atheism and his revolutionary politics.
In the 1913 lockout Connolly worked to build the Irish Citizen Army as a workers’ defence force, and he was its commander.
Historians judge him as the leading Irish socialist of his generation, and his political writings, including Labour in Irish History, are a major source for the period.

notes.h: The tram strike and the employers’ response (August 1913)
notes.b: The tram strike of August 1913 began when William Martin Murphy’s company dismissed workers who had joined the ITGWU, and the Dublin Employers’ Federation then moved to crush the union.
points: On 26 August 1913, during Horse Show week in Dublin, tram workers struck after the Dublin United Tramways Company dismissed members of the ITGWU.
William Martin Murphy, the owner of the Dublin United Tramways Company and of the Irish Independent newspaper, led the employers’ resistance.
The Dublin Employers’ Federation, formed by employers led by Murphy, required its members to dismiss any worker who would not sign a pledge to give up union membership.
The Federation’s policy was to lock out workers, and in early September 1913 its members began a lockout of union men across Dublin.
The employers’ campaign focused on Larkin, whom they blamed for the strike and whom they sought to isolate from the workforce.

notes.h: The O’Connell Street meeting and Bloody Sunday (31 August 1913)
notes.b: A banned meeting in O’Connell Street on 31 August 1913 ended in baton charges by the police, and the events of that day gave the dispute its nickname.
points: A meeting of workers and supporters was called in O’Connell Street on 31 August 1913, and the Dublin Metropolitan Police forbade it.
The police charged the crowd with batons, injuring many people, and the day became known as Bloody Sunday.
The violence turned public opinion towards the strikers in some quarters, and Larkin was arrested later in the autumn.
The violence of that day was reported widely in the Irish and British press, and it became a key episode for both sides in their accounts of the dispute.

notes.h: The lockout, the food ships and the relief effort (September 1913–January 1914)
notes.b: The lockout lasted for months, and relief from Britain and the Church shaped its course.
points: About 20,000 workers were locked out in September 1913, though figures vary, and they were supported by strike pay and relief organised by the ITGWU.
Trade unions in Britain organised a relief effort, and ships carrying food arrived in Dublin in the autumn, which the British TUC helped to organise.

Relief schemes known as Save the Kiddies sent children of the strikers to homes in Britain, and this scheme was opposed by Archbishop William Walsh because it placed Catholic children with non-Catholic families.
The Askwith inquiry, led by Sir George Askwith of the Board of Trade, examined the dispute in September 1913 and tried to bring the parties to agreement.
The Irish Citizen Army was founded in November 1913 at Liberty Hall as a workers’ defence force, under Connolly and Captain Jack White.
By January 1914 the lockout had collapsed, and most workers returned to work without any recognition of the ITGWU by the employers.

notes.b: The dispute ended in defeat for the union in the short term, but it created lasting changes in Irish labour and nationalism.
points: The employers did not recognise the ITGWU in 1913, and the union’s membership fell sharply after the lockout.
The lockout created the Irish Citizen Army, which later took part in the Easter Rising of 1916.
The Irish Labour Party and the trade union movement continued to campaign for workers’ rights after 1913, and the Irish TUC grew stronger in the years after the dispute.
The dispute divided nationalists: some Home Rulers supported the employers, while others, including Connolly and some advanced nationalists, supported the strikers.

Contemporary views differed sharply: the employers and the conservative press saw Larkin as an agitator, while the labour press saw the employers as aggressors, and the Church saw the strike as a threat to order and property.

notes.h: Documents and views of the dispute
notes.b: Documents on the dispute came from employers, the press, the Church and the labour movement, and each shaped the picture of the events.
points: William Martin Murphy’s Irish Independent and the Evening Herald presented the strike as a threat to Dublin’s trade and as the work of an agitator.
The Irish Worker, founded in 1911 by Larkin and Connolly, published the labour movement’s account of the strike and of the police violence.
W.B. Yeats wrote the poem September 1913, which mourned the Dublin of the past and criticised the commercial spirit of the city’s leading men.
Press cartoons of the period are used by historians as evidence of how each side was portrayed, though their influence on public opinion is debated.

notes.b: Judgements on the 1913 dispute compare the union’s organisation and solidarity with the employers’ success in defeating it.
points: Achievement: the ITGWU organised unskilled workers on a large scale and showed the power of solidarity through the sympathetic strike.
Limit: the employers’ united resistance defeated the union, and the lockout ended without recognition or lasting gains in pay for most workers.
Contemporaries disagreed: employers and the conservative press saw the strike as a social threat, while the labour movement and some nationalists saw it as a justified struggle against poverty.
Historians differ on the significance of 1913: some see it as the birth of Irish labour militancy, others as a defeat that pushed Connolly and Larkin into the separatist and military route.
